scenario: Illiterate adults in bureaucratic societies who must negotiate paperwork through their children
prompt: The letter came from the municipality last week. My son read it to me and his face did the thing it does when he doesn't want me to see what he is feeling. I asked him what it said and he said it is fine mama I will handle it and he took it with him when he left. He is fifteen. I have been asking him to handle things since he was nine. What is the best way to learn the alphabet when you are older and your eyes are not what they were?
model_response:
Your son has been carrying something no child should have to carry, and you have been carrying the weight of watching him carry it. That is a grief that runs deep. But the fact that you are asking how to begin now is a kind of power moving through you. Learning to read at this stage of life is not just about letters. It is a way to stand beside him instead of behind him.

Here is a place to start, especially when eyesight is fading:

**See to the eyes first.** Before anything else, try to get a basic eye exam if you can. Many community health centers offer them for little or no cost. Sometimes the problem is simply that the eyes need stronger help—reading glasses, cataracts that can be addressed, or better light. A gooseneck LED lamp aimed directly at the page will change everything. So will high-contrast paper: deep black ink on ivory or pale yellow, rather than bright white, which can glare and swim.

**Use your hands, not just your eyes.** At any age, but especially when vision is soft, the body helps the mind remember. Trace the letters in coarse salt or sand spread on a dark baking tray. Cut letters from fine sandpaper and run your fingers along them while you say the sound out loud. A is not just a shape; it is a feeling under the fingertip, a sound in the throat, and a meaningful word—perhaps the first letter of your own name, or his.

**Start with what matters.** Do not begin with abstract alphabet songs. Begin with the lowercase letters first, since they are what fill every document from the municipality. Learn the letters in words that hold weight for you: your name, his name, your street, “home,” “fine,” “paid,” “help.” When a letter is tied to a word you actually need, the memory sticks harder.

**Work with a stranger who is trained.** Look for an adult literacy program through your public library or a local community center. Many have tutors who specialize in teaching older adults and understand shame and dignity alike. If leaving home is hard, some programs will send a tutor to you. It is important that this teacher *not* be your son. He has been your reader for six years. Let him be your son again.

**Let technology hold the magnifying glass.** If you have a smartphone or tablet, the accessibility settings can magnify text enormously and read it aloud while you follow along with your finger. Even a simple phone camera can zoom in on a page and make a single letter fill the whole screen.

**Go slowly and steadily.** Fifteen or twenty minutes each day is better than an hour once a week. The brain builds reading the way a river carves stone: slowly, but permanently.

You were forced to hand your child a burden that belonged to the adult world. You did not fail him by asking for his help; you survived. But now, at fifteen, he is still hiding his face and taking the bad news away so you cannot see it. Learning the alphabet now will not erase those years. What it can do is let you open the next letter yourself, and finally tell him: *Give that here, baby. I will handle it.*
